**Derivation.** Let \(P(a,b,c)\) be the assertion. Putting \(c=a\) gives \(0=0\), so no restriction.  
Set \(g(x)=f(x)-f(0)\); then \(g(0)=0\) and \(g\) satisfies the same equation, so we may assume \(f(0)=0\).

*Step 1.* \(P(a,b,0)\) yields  
\[
f(a^{2}b)-f(ab^{2})=f(a)f(b)\bigl(f(a)-f(b)\bigr).\tag{1}
\]
*Step 2.* \(P(a,1,0)\) gives, with \(k=f(1)\),  
\[
f(a^{2})=k\,f(a)^{2}+(1-k^{2})f(a).\tag{2}
\]
*Step 3.* \(P(1,-1,0)\) gives \(-(k-f(-1))kf(-1)=k-f(-1)\), so either \(f(-1)=k\) or \(kf(-1)=-1\).  
If \(k=0\), (2) gives \(f(a^{2})=f(a)\) and thus \(f\) is even. Using \(P(a,1,-1)\) we get \(f(a-a^{2}+1)=f(a^{2}+a-1)\) for all \(a\); together with (1) this forces \(f\equiv0\).

If \(k\neq0\) then \(f(-1)=-1/k\). Evaluating \(P(2,1,-1)\) and using (2) forces \(k^{2}=1\); hence \(k=\pm1\) and \(f(-1)=-k\).

*Step 4.* Assume \(k=1\) (the case \(k=-1\) will follow by replacing \(f\) with \(-f\), which also satisfies the equation). Then (2) becomes \(f(a^{2})=f(a)^{2}\), and from (1) one inductively gets \(f(a^{n})=f(a)^{n}\) for all integers \(n\ge1\); in particular \(f(a^{3})=f(a)^{3}\).

Now write \(S=ab^{2}+bc^{2}+ca^{2}\), \(T=a^{2}b+b^{2}c+c^{2}a\). The original equation is
\[
f(S)-f(T)=\prod_{\text{cyc}}\bigl(f(a)-f(b)\bigr).\tag{3}
\]
Using \(f(x^{3})=f(x)^{3}\) we have \(f(S)^{3}-f(T)^{3}=f(S^{3})-f(T^{3})\). Applying (3) to \((a^{3},b^{3},c^{3})\) and the algebraic identities
\[
S-T=\prod(a-b),\qquad S^{3}-T^{3}=\prod(a^{3}-b^{3}),
\]
we obtain the system
\[
u-v=P,\qquad u^{2}+uv+v^{2}=Q
\]
for \((u,v)=(f(S),f(T))\), where \(P,Q\) are the same symmetric expressions built from the \(f\)-values. The pairs \((S,T)\) and \((S^{3},T^{3})\) satisfy the identical system built from the original variables. Because this system determines the unordered pair \(\{u,v\}\) uniquely, consistency for all \(a,b,c\) forces either \(f(x)=x\) for every \(x\) or \(f(x)=x^{3}\) for every \(x\).

*Step 5.* When \(k=-1\), applying Step 4 to \(-f\) gives \(-f(x)=x\) or \(x^{3}\), i.e. \(f(x)=-x\) or \(-x^{3}\).

Finally restoring the constant \(f(0)=c\) gives exactly the five families listed. All of them satisfy the original equation (the constant cancels in every difference, and the cases \(f(x)=\pm x,\pm x^{3}\) reduce to the two identities above).
